nameStory: This bee gets its 'silky' name from the lustrous, almost metallic sheen on its body that catches the light like fine silk fabric. The 'striped' part comes from the bold yellow and black bands across its abdomen, while 'sweat bee' refers to the family's habit of landing on people to lap up salt from perspiration.
description: The Silky Striped Sweat Bee is a small, eye-catching native bee with a brilliant metallic green head and thorax that shimmers in sunlight. Its abdomen features distinctive yellow and black stripes that make it look like a tiny flying zebra. These solitary bees are about the size of a small paper clip, making them much smaller than honeybees. Despite their small size, their metallic coloring makes them surprisingly easy to spot when they're visiting flowers.

idTips.label: Metallic Green Sheen
idTips.description: The head and thorax gleam with a brilliant metallic green color that shifts and shimmers as the bee moves, almost like looking at an iridescent beetle

idTips.label: Striped Abdomen
idTips.description: Bold alternating yellow and black stripes across the rounded abdomen, creating a distinct banded pattern that's visible even when the bee is in motion

idTips.label: Small Size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than a honeybee, about the length of your pinky nail, with a compact, robust build

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with quick, darting movements between flowers, often hovering briefly before landing with a gentle buzzing sound

idTips.label: Flower Preference
idTips.description: Most commonly seen on small, open flowers like asters and goldenrod where they can easily access nectar with their short tongues

habitat: Look for Silky Striped Sweat Bees in sunny, open areas throughout New England including meadows, gardens, parks, and field edges. They prefer areas with diverse wildflowers and are often found near sandy or well-drained soils where they can excavate their ground nests. You'll spot them most often in suburban gardens and natural areas with abundant late-season blooms.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but they're not yet common. Early individuals may be seen on spring wildflowers like wild lupine.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in mid to late summer when adults are most abundant and easily observed. Look for them actively foraging on a wide variety of flowers during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Still active into early fall, especially on late-blooming flowers like asters and goldenrod. This is often the best time to observe them as they're focused on building up energy reserves.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frost. The species overwinters as larvae in underground nest cells, invisible to casual observers.

funFact: Unlike honeybees that live in huge colonies, female Silky Striped Sweat Bees are solo architects who excavate their own underground tunnels up to 6 inches deep, complete with multiple side chambers where they create individual 'baby food' balls of pollen and nectar for each egg they lay.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other striped sweat bees in the same genus, but the Silky Striped Sweat Bee's brilliant metallic green head and thorax set it apart from the duller Bicolored Striped Sweat Bee. Remember: if it looks like it's wearing a shimmery green jacket with yellow-striped pants, it's likely the silky species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'sweat bee,' these insects are completely harmless and rarely sting unless directly handled or trapped. Their attraction to human perspiration is simply because they need salt and minerals for their diet, not because they're aggressive.
compareHints: Among its Agapostemon relatives, the Silky Striped Sweat Bee has the most pronounced metallic green coloration on the head and thorax. The Bicolored Striped Sweat Bee has a duller, less reflective green, while the Brown-winged Striped Sweat Bee has noticeably darker, brownish wing membranes. The Fine Striped Sweat Bee is smaller with more delicate, narrower stripes on the abdomen.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its striped sweat bee relatives, the Bicolored Striped Sweat Bee is the most commonly encountered in New England.
